opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, the biggest change is that my job has shifted from *doing* the work to *directing* it.

A couple of years ago, if I wanted to explore an idea, say prototype a feature or dig through a messy dataset, I'd block off an afternoon and grind through it myself. Now I'll write down what I'm trying to figure out, hand it to an agent, and it'll read the codebase, run things, hit errors, fix them, and come back with something concrete. My time goes into framing the problem well and then judging what comes back.

That sounds like a small change, but it's had a few effects I didn't expect.

First, the cost of trying things has collapsed. I used to be quite careful about which ideas I pursued, because each one was expensive. Now I'll often run three or four directions in parallel just to see which one has legs. So I've become more experimental, and frankly I think my taste matters more now than my raw execution speed.

Second, it's changed what "being good at your job" means. Clear writing has become a technical skill. If I can't explain what I want, including the constraints and what "done" looks like, the agent will happily go off and build the wrong thing very efficiently. A lot of my day is now writing specs, reviewing diffs, and asking "why did you do it this way?"

Third, and this is the part I'm still working out, there's a question of trust and verification. The agent is often right, which makes it tempting to stop checking. But the failures tend to be subtle: plausible-looking code with a wrong assumption buried in it. So I've had to build habits around tests, small reviewable steps, and keeping a human in the loop for anything irreversible.

So overall I'd say it feels less like using a tool and more like managing a very fast, very tireless collaborator who needs good direction. The leverage is enormous, but it rewards people who think clearly about what they actually want.

r001.rationale: The response describes a shift from doing work to directing agents, but it does not say this overhaul happened over roughly two weeks.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the biggest shift isn't that I write less code. It's that I spend my day in a different mode entirely.

Before, my working rhythm was: think about a problem, open the editor, implement, test, fix, repeat. Most of my hours were inside that loop. Now I describe what I want, the agent goes and does it, and I come back twenty minutes later to a pull request with tests. My job becomes reviewing, steering, and deciding what's worth building in the first place. That sounds like a small change, but it changes what kind of thinking fills your day.

A few concrete things I've noticed.

First, I'm much more willing to try things. If exploring an idea used to cost me half a day, I'd think hard about whether it was worth it, and often I'd just not do it. Now the cost of a prototype is a paragraph of instructions and some waiting. So I run three or four experiments in parallel and throw away the ones that don't work. The bar for "let's just see" has dropped a lot.

Second, I've had to get much better at describing intent. The agent is very good at execution, but it executes what you asked, not what you meant. So the skill that matters now is being precise about constraints, about what "done" looks like, about what you don't want touched. I've basically become a better tech lead because I'm forced to write down things I used to keep in my head.

Third, there's a trust calibration that takes time. Early on I read every line it produced, which defeats the purpose. Later I learned where I can relax and where I can't. Boilerplate, migrations, test scaffolding, I barely look. Anything touching money, auth, or data deletion, I read carefully and I ask it to explain its reasoning. It's similar to how you learn to work with a new colleague.

The honest downside is that the bottleneck moved to me. The agent can produce faster than I can review well. Some days I feel like I'm the slow part of the system, and that's a strange feeling for an engineer. I don't think that's fully solved yet, for me or for anyone.

So if I had to sum it up: it didn't replace the work, it changed what the work is. More judgment, less typing. And for me, the judgment part was always the interesting part anyway.

r001.rationale: The response describes a major change in Kay Ke’s work process, but it does not say the overhaul happened over roughly two weeks.

astra-6.text:
I see Claude Agent shifting my work from doing every step myself to deciding what to delegate and how to judge the result. That puts more emphasis on framing the problem: What am I trying to achieve? What context matters? What does a good outcome look like?

The potential is to spend less time on routine execution and more time on decisions. But delegation still takes attention. I need to understand the output well enough to challenge it and take responsibility for what I use.

r001.rationale: The response describes a shift toward delegating and judging results, but does not say Kay Ke overhauled their entire work process or that this happened over roughly two weeks.
